prompt: SDLC (software development life cycle) is a structured sequence of phases a software system moves through, from the first idea all the way to eventual retirement.
What does SDLC describe?
explanation: It's a structured sequence of phases (software development lifecycle) — from idea to retirement.

prompt: SDLC covers a system from idea to retirement.
SDLC stands for software development ___.
What is SDLC made up of?
A defined process catches problems earlier and makes work repeatable, instead of every project reinventing how it gets built.
What does a defined process help catch?
explanation: A defined process also keeps work repeatable, instead of reinventing things each time.

prompt: Ad-hoc coding makes work more repeatable.
explanation: A defined process is what makes work repeatable, not ad-hoc coding.

prompt: Process makes work more ___.
What does ad-hoc coding risk?
Nearly every SDLC model builds on the same core phases in some form: requirements, design, build, test, deploy, and maintain.
Pick core SDLC phases.
explanation: The full list of core phases: requirements, design, build, test, deploy, and maintain.

prompt: Maintenance is one of the core SDLC phases.
Nearly every model shares the same core ___.
Name a core SDLC phase.
Gathering requirements means finding out what a system actually needs to do, from the people who will use or depend on it, before building it.
What does requirements gathering find out?
explanation: It comes from real users, gathered before building starts.

prompt: Requirements should be gathered before building starts.
Requirements come from the people who ___ it.
Who is a good source of requirements?
Functional requirements describe what a system must do; non-functional requirements describe how well it must do it, like speed or security.
What do functional requirements describe?
explanation: Non-functional requirements, by contrast, describe how well it performs — like its speed or security.

prompt: Speed is a non-functional requirement.
Non-functional requirements cover how ___ a system performs.
Give an example non-functional requirement.
A user story describes a need from a user's point of view, and acceptance criteria say exactly how you will know it has been met.
What does a user story describe?
explanation: Its acceptance criteria say exactly how you'll know that need has been met — the done state.

prompt: Acceptance criteria say how you know a story is met.
A user story is written from the ___ view.
What do acceptance criteria define?
A feasibility analysis checks whether a project is realistically worth doing, before committing real time and money to it.
What does feasibility analysis check?
explanation: It happens before real money is spent, so resources aren't wasted.

prompt: Feasibility analysis happens before real resources are spent.
Feasibility analysis happens ___ real spending.
What does feasibility analysis avoid?
High-level design sketches a system's overall shape, and low-level design works out its detailed internals afterward.
What does high-level design sketch?
explanation: Low-level design comes after, working out the detailed internals — it's the more detailed of the two.

prompt: Low-level design comes after high-level design.
Low-level design works out detailed ___.
Which is more detailed?
A design document records the plan for a system's structure before code gets written, so the team agrees on the approach first.
When is a design document written?
explanation: It also helps the team agree on the approach before any code exists.

prompt: A design document helps a team agree on an approach.
A design document records the ___ before coding.
What does a design document describe?
A prototype is a rough, disposable version built to test an idea quickly and cheaply before committing to building the real thing.
What is a prototype meant to be?
explanation: It exists to test an idea quickly and cheaply, which is also why it's usually discarded rather than kept.

prompt: A prototype is meant to test an idea.
A prototype is often ___.
Why build a prototype first?
Coding standards are shared conventions that keep a codebase consistent across many contributors, instead of everyone writing however they like.
What do coding standards keep consistent?
explanation: That consistency holds across every contributor working in the codebase, not just one.

prompt: Coding standards are shared across contributors.
Standards apply across ___ contributors.
What happens without shared standards?
Version control sits throughout the whole SDLC, tracking every change to code from the first commit through every later release.
What does version control track?
explanation: It runs throughout the whole SDLC, starting from the very first commit.

prompt: Version control is used only at the very end.
explanation: It runs throughout the whole SDLC, not just at the end.

prompt: Version control runs ___ the SDLC.
When does version control tracking start?
A code review is a teammate checking your code before it merges, catching issues while they are still cheap to fix.
When does a code review happen?
explanation: It's a teammate reviewing your code, catching issues while they're still cheap to fix.

prompt: Code review catches issues while they are cheap to fix.
A ___ checks your code before it merges.
Why review code before merging?
Pair programming has two developers working on the same code together in real time, one typing while the other reviews as they go.
How many developers work together in a pair?
explanation: They work together in real time — one types while the other reviews live.

prompt: Pair programming happens in real time together.
One person types while the other ___.
What happens as the pair works?
Testing is not just one phase tacked onto the end; it belongs throughout the whole SDLC, from early requirements onward.
Testing belongs ___ the SDLC, not just the end.
explanation: Testing belongs throughout the whole cycle, starting from early requirements onward — treating it as one final phase is a common mistake.

prompt: Testing belongs ___ the whole SDLC.
When can testing start?
Treating testing as one final phase is a common mistake.
Unit tests check one function, integration tests check parts working together, system tests check the whole product, and acceptance tests check it against real needs.
What does a system test check?
explanation: Unit tests check one function, integration tests check parts working together, and acceptance tests check it against real needs.

prompt: Acceptance tests check against real needs.
A unit test checks one ___.
What does an integration test check?
TDD means writing a failing test first, then writing just enough code to make it pass, before cleaning things up.
What comes first in TDD?
explanation: After that failing test, you write just enough code to make it pass.

prompt: TDD writes just enough code to pass the test.
TDD writes the ___ before the code.
What is the first TDD test meant to do?
Blue-green swaps traffic to a whole new environment at once; canary slowly shifts a small slice of traffic to test a new version first, both aim to reduce release risk.
What does canary do first?
explanation: Blue-green instead swaps traffic to a whole new environment at once — both approaches exist to reduce release risk.

prompt: Blue-green switches traffic to a whole new environment.
Canary tests a small ___ of traffic first.
What do both strategies aim to reduce?
Continuous integration means merging and testing code changes frequently, in small batches, instead of one huge merge at the end.
How often does CI merge changes?
explanation: It also runs tests on each change, avoiding one huge merge at the end.

prompt: CI merges changes in small batches.
CI avoids one huge merge at the ___.
What does CI run on each change?
Continuous delivery keeps every change ready to release with a manual final step; continuous deployment releases every passing change automatically.
What does continuous deployment do automatically?
explanation: Continuous delivery, by contrast, keeps a manual release step — deployment auto-releases every passing change, fully automated end to end.

prompt: Continuous delivery still has a manual release step.
Continuous deployment releases every ___ change.
Which one is fully automated end to end?
Release management plans and coordinates exactly what ships and when, so a release is deliberate instead of accidental.
What does release management coordinate?
explanation: That makes a release deliberate, not accidental.

prompt: A release should be deliberate, not accidental.
Release management plans exactly what ___.
What is the opposite of a planned release?
Software gets changed after shipping for four reasons: fixing bugs, adapting to a new environment, adding new capability, or preventing future problems before they happen.
Pick reasons for post-ship maintenance.
explanation: A fourth reason: adapting to a new environment, like a platform or OS update.

prompt: Software can be changed to adapt to a new environment.
Maintenance happens ___ a system first ships.
Give an example maintenance reason.
Monitoring watches a live system so problems are found before users have to report them themselves.
What does monitoring help find early?
explanation: It watches the live system continuously — the weak alternative is just waiting for users to complain.

prompt: Monitoring can catch a problem before users report it.
Monitoring watches a ___ system continuously.
What is a weak alternative to monitoring?
When something breaks for real users right now, the priority is restoring service first, and doing the full root-cause dig afterward.
What is the first priority during an incident?
explanation: The deeper root-cause investigation happens afterward, once service is back up.

prompt: Root-cause analysis can happen after service is restored.
During an incident, restoring service comes ___.
When does deep root-cause work usually happen?
Deprecating a feature means retiring it deliberately, with a warning, a timeline, and a plan, instead of just quietly letting it rot unmaintained.
How should a feature be retired?
explanation: That means a warning to users, a timeline, and a plan — not silently letting it rot.

prompt: Deprecation usually includes a warning to users.
Deprecation avoids letting a feature quietly ___.
What should a deprecation plan include?
The Waterfall model moves strictly through phases in sequence, where each one finishes fully before the next begins, so a late change once a phase is done is hard to absorb.
How does Waterfall move through phases?
explanation: That strict order also makes late changes hard to absorb once a phase is already done.

prompt: In Waterfall, a phase finishes before the next begins.
Waterfall is a strictly ___ model.
What can Waterfall struggle with?

The V-Model extends Waterfall by pairing each development phase with a matching test phase; test planning happens alongside each dev phase, drawn as a V shape with dev phases going down one side and test phases coming up the other.
What does the V-Model pair with each dev phase?
explanation: It extends the Waterfall model, and gets its name from the V shape this pairing draws.

prompt: The V-Model extends the Waterfall idea.
Test planning happens ___ development in the V-Model.
What shape gives the V-Model its name?
The Iterative model builds a system in repeated cycles, improving it a little more with each pass instead of all at once.
How does the Iterative model improve a system?
explanation: It avoids building the whole system at once, favoring small repeated passes instead.

prompt: Each iteration improves the system a bit more.
The Iterative model uses repeated ___.
What does the Iterative model avoid?
The Spiral model combines iteration with an explicit risk-analysis step at the start of every single cycle.
What does Spiral add to iteration?
explanation: That risk-analysis step happens at the start of every single cycle, not just once.

prompt: Risk analysis happens every cycle in the Spiral model.
Spiral pairs iteration with explicit ___ analysis.
When does risk analysis happen in Spiral?
The Agile model delivers working software in short, frequent cycles, adjusting based on feedback as it comes in.
What does Agile deliver in short cycles?
explanation: Those cycles are short and frequent, adjusting based on feedback as it comes in.

prompt: Agile adjusts based on ongoing feedback.
Agile cycles are short and ___.
What drives changes in the Agile model?
DevOps evolved from the traditional SDLC's separate dev and ops teams, merging them into one shared responsibility so software ships and runs faster and more reliably.
What does DevOps merge?
explanation: It evolved from the traditional SDLC's separate dev and ops teams, aiming for faster, more reliable delivery.

prompt: DevOps aims for faster, more reliable delivery.
DevOps treats dev and ops as ___ responsibility.
What does DevOps evolve from?
Useful documentation gets kept at every phase of the SDLC, not just dumped as one pile of docs at the very end.
When should documentation be kept?
explanation: Not just dumped as one pile of docs at the very end.

prompt: Documentation should only appear at the very end.
explanation: Useful documentation is kept at every phase, not dumped all at the end.

prompt: Documentation should be ___, not a big dump.
What is a weak documentation habit?
Compliance work keeps a traceable record of decisions and changes for real accountability, especially important for regulated or high-stakes systems.
What does an audit trail keep?
explanation: It matters especially for regulated or high-stakes systems, giving real accountability.

prompt: Audit trails matter more for regulated systems.
An audit trail records past ___.
Why does compliance matter for high-stakes systems?
The right SDLC model matches a project's actual risk, size, and how well its requirements are already understood, not one universal best answer.
What should drive the choice of SDLC model?
explanation: It also depends on how well-understood the requirements already are — there's no single universal best answer.

prompt: There is one universal best SDLC model for everyone.
explanation: The right fit depends on the specific project, not one universal answer.

prompt: Fit the model to the project's actual ___.
What matters when picking a model?
Which is preventive maintenance?
Order the core SDLC phases.
Order the test levels, narrowest first.
Order the TDD steps.
options: Write a failing test|Write code to pass it|Clean up the code

prompt: Order a CI cycle's steps.
options: Make a small change|Merge into main|Automated tests run

prompt: Order Waterfall's phases.
Order the V-Model, down then up.
